title: ITU-T Recommendations Q.23 and Q.24: DTMF Sending and Reception
access: Full official reading access to Q.23 (11/1988) and Q.24 (11/1988), both listed by ITU-T as in force. The recommendations remain ITU-copyrighted; this dossier stores only citation metadata and paraphrased findings, not redistributed standard text.
topics: Q.23 §§6–7 and Fig. 1/Q.23: DTMF uses one simultaneous tone from a low group (697, 770, 852, 941 Hz) and one from a high group (1209, 1336, 1477, 1633 Hz), allocated to sixteen keypad symbols.
Q.23 §7: each transmitted frequency must remain within ±1.8% of nominal and total harmonic/intermodulation products must be at least 20 dB below the fundamentals.

Q.24 §§2.2–2.5: a receiver checks for exactly one frequency from each group and must consider frequency tolerance, received levels and inter-group level difference, valid-signal duration, short-signal rejection, pauses, and brief interruptions.
Q.24 Annex A: example operational values vary by administration and application; the recommendation does not establish one universal timing/twist threshold table.
key_results: A valid symbol requires simultaneous evidence for one and only one low-group tone and one and only one high-group tone; a lone tone or two tones from the same group must not decode.
The sending frequency set and ±1.8% tolerance are defined in Q.23, while Q.24 treats receiver tolerance and transmission impairment as deployment-dependent engineering parameters.
Receiver timing is a decision rule with both acceptance and rejection boundaries; implementation thresholds must name the administration/application profile rather than claiming universality.
pedagogy: Use the standards after the DSP detector is derived: learners map the two-group code to resonator/Goertzel measurements, then convert qualitative receiver obligations into an explicit test profile. Keep normative source facts separate from course-selected thresholds and expose speech simulation, twist, detuning, and finite-duration false detections.
figures: Draw a new rights-safe 4-by-4 keypad/frequency matrix from the cited numeric groups; do not reproduce Figure 1/Q.23.
Draw a receiver decision table separating exactly-one-per-group validity, frequency tolerance, level/twist policy, duration, pause, and interruption tests.
gems: Q.24 separates fundamental receiver parameters from the numerical values adopted by administrations, preventing a course laboratory threshold from being mislabeled as a universal ITU mandate.
The exactly-one-per-group rule supplies a stronger falsification test than simple energy detection: two loud same-group tones are invalid even though two target filters fire.
chapter_map: Sending frequencies, keypad allocation, tolerance, and distortion → Q.23 §§6–7 and Fig. 1/Q.23.
Receiver pair validity, tolerance, level/twist, and timing categories → Q.24 §§2.2–2.5.
Example administration values and non-universality → Q.24 Annex A.
